strengths: Principled Theoretical Formulation: The paper establishes a rigorous reduction theorem (Theorem 3.3) showing that four natural physical principles—locality, permutation equivariance, orientation covariance, and passivity/energy balance—uniquely determine the signed-incidence structure of the conservative coupling J, isolating learnable components strictly to the metric G and dissipation R.

Comprehensive and Multi-Faceted Evaluation: The empirical evaluation goes well beyond standard MSE metrics, testing energy drift, dispersion relations, canonical consistency, equipartition, momentum conservation, out-of-distribution transfer (frequency, wave speed, resolution), and acoustic scattering data from The Well benchmark.

Thorough Ablations and Diagnostics: The ablation experiments in Section C.7 directly test the theoretical assumptions by isolating the impact of dropping orientation covariance, scrambling topology, and removing metric positive-definiteness, confirming the necessity of each design constraint.

Computational Efficiency: By leveraging sparse incidence matrices and learning only lightweight metric-parameterizing MLPs, MeshFT-Net achieves significantly lower parameter counts, faster training/inference latency, and lower memory footprint compared to dense or unconstrained GNN baselines.
weaknesses: Scope Dominated by Wave and Linear Dynamics: Most empirical benchmarks focus on wave-type problems (linear acoustics, plane waves, damped waves, and acoustic scattering) where DEC/FDTD formulations naturally excel. Applications to complex nonlinear mechanics (e.g., Navier-Stokes fluids, large-strain plasticity, contact) where standard MeshGraphNets are commonly benchmarked remain largely unexplored beyond a small toy shallow-water experiment.

Assumptions Underlying Lemma A.1: The proof of the local reduction relies heavily on linearity in Lemma A.1 when characterizing admissible cell interactions. While the Jacobian reduction is stated locally, clarifying how strongly this restricts genuinely nonlinear vector fields before linearization would improve theoretical transparency.

Model Capacity and Expressivity Comparison: In the linear experiments, MeshFT-Net has only 642 parameters and primarily learns local Hodge star diagonal scales, essentially acting as a parameter estimation scheme for a classical structure-preserving numerical integrator. While this explains its superior stability, it raises questions about how well the framework scales to highly expressive, complex surrogate modeling tasks without sacrificing its structural guarantees.

strengths: Sound theoretical foundation: The paper presents an elegant and rigorous reduction theorem (Theorem 3.3) showing that minimal physical requirements—locality, permutation equivariance, orientation covariance, and energy balance/passivity—uniquely dictate the Jacobian-level structure into a port–Hamiltonian form with incidence-based conservative coupling.

Principled architecture design: Rather than postulating an arbitrary black-box GNN or an unconstrained port-Hamiltonian system, MeshFT-Net directly operationalizes the theory by fixing the topology-driven signed incidence matrix and confining learning strictly to metric and dissipation operators.

Comprehensive physical diagnostics: The empirical evaluation goes well beyond standard one-step MSE by systematically measuring physical fidelity diagnostics, including wave-speed dispersion, canonical momentum consistency, discrete PDE residuals, energy equipartition, and momentum conservation.

Strong out-of-distribution (OOD) and ablation results: The model exhibits remarkably stable rollout behavior under shifts in frequency, resolution, and wave speed. The ablation experiments (Table 9) carefully isolate and validate the role of orientation covariance, topology preservation, and metric positive-definiteness.
weaknesses: Limited practical empirical scope: While the reduction theorem is formulated broadly, the core experiments and the primary architecture of MeshFT-Net focus overwhelmingly on linear wave/acoustic equations with state-independent incidence coupling. The evaluation lacks validation on complex nonlinear continuum systems (e.g., Navier-Stokes fluids, plastic deformation, or shock waves).

Under-evaluated realistic benchmark: For the real-world dataset (The Well acoustic scattering), the evaluation is notably brief: only qualitative snapshots are shown in Figure 3, without accompanying quantitative rollout error metrics or direct baseline comparisons in the main text.

Close connection to prior discrete exterior calculus (DEC) methods: Data-driven DEC (e.g., Trask et al., 2022) already advocates fixing topological coboundaries $D_k$ and learning metric Hodge stars. Although this paper derives this split from port-Hamiltonian principles and physical symmetries, the resulting practical algorithm for linear wave equations closely resembles established structure-preserving DEC discretizations, somewhat limiting the novelty of the realized architecture.

Gap between theorem generality and architecture realization: Theorem 3.3 permits state-dependent conservative coupling ($C_k(z)$), but the main model defaults to state-independent coupling (Corollary 3.4). While Section 5.5 presents a small 2D shallow-water toy experiment, state-dependent coupling on general meshes remains largely undeveloped and untested.

strengths: Principled theoretical reduction: Rather than postulating a port–Hamiltonian template heuristically, Theorem 3.3 derives the port–Hamiltonian structure and signed-incidence coupling directly from fundamental physical principles (locality, permutation equivariance, orientation covariance, and passivity). The proof cleanly shows how orientation covariance rules out same-degree adjacency terms.

Exact structure preservation: By fixing the signed coboundary operators D_k in the interconnection matrix J, the model mechanically preserves topological invariants (such as D_{k+1} D_k = 0, discrete Gauss laws, and momentum) and guarantees energy non-increase by construction without relying on fragile soft PDE penalty losses.

Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation: The empirical validation thoroughly probes physical fidelity through well-chosen diagnostics (wave speed/dispersion, canonical consistency, PDE residuals, equipartition, momentum conservation), extensive out-of-distribution tests (frequency, resolution transfer, parameter shifts), and data efficiency tests.

High computational and parameter efficiency: As demonstrated in Table 10, MeshFT-Net achieves substantially lower long-horizon error while using orders of magnitude fewer parameters (642 parameters vs. >100k for baselines) and displaying lower latency and peak memory footprint due to sparse, incidence-based operations.

Insightful ablations: Appendix C.7 systematically disables individual theoretical components (orientation, topology wiring, metric positive-definiteness), empirically validating that each requirement in the reduction theorem is critical to avoiding energy blowup and unphysical modes.
weaknesses: Predominance of linear and mildly nonlinear benchmarks: The majority of the quantitative evaluation centers on 2D linear wave propagation, damped linear waves, and linear acoustic scattering. While Section 5.5 and Appendix C.6 provide a toy shallow-water setup, broader testing on challenging nonlinear continuum mechanics problems (e.g., advection-dominated flows, shocks, or large-strain elastodynamics) would further substantiate the generality of the method.

Simplification to state-independent interconnection in the primary model: Although Theorem 3.3 accommodates state-dependent gains C_k(z), the main MeshFT-Net implementation relies on Corollary 3.4's state-independent interconnection. For many complex nonlinear continuum systems, state-dependent coupling is essential, and the current empirical demonstration of state-dependent J is limited to a small toy experiment.

strengths: Principled and elegant theoretical foundation: Rather than postulating an ad-hoc global Hamiltonian or port-Hamiltonian architecture, the paper proves a reduction theorem (Theorem 3.3) demonstrating that four basic physical requirements (locality, permutation equivariance, orientation covariance, and passivity/energy balance) necessitate a local port-Hamiltonian decomposition where conservative coupling is structurally fixed to signed incidence operators (mesh topology) and only metric/dissipative terms are learned.

Comprehensive and rigorous experimental evaluation: The authors evaluate MeshFT-Net across a wide variety of tasks, including analytic wave benchmarks on regular and Delaunay grids, real acoustic scattering from The Well, irregular heterogeneous elastodynamics, and multiple nonlinear lattice benchmarks (FPU, damped phi-4, Sine-Gordon).

Detailed physics-informed diagnostics: Beyond standard MSE metrics, the paper rigorously measures physical consistency via wave dispersion, canonical consistency, PDE residuals, kinetic-potential equipartition, and momentum conservation, demonstrating orders-of-magnitude improvements in long-horizon stability and conservation over competitive baselines (MGN, MGN-HP, HNN, FNO, GraphCON, and PI-MGN).

Extensive ablation studies: The paper includes thoughtful ablations isolating the exact roles of topological signed incidence, orientation covariance, metric positive-definiteness, and state-dependent vs. fixed interconnection coupling, empirically validating each component of the reduction theorem.

Computational efficiency: MeshFT-Net leverages sparse matrix-vector operations with O(N) complexity and shows superior parameter efficiency, faster training/inference wall-clock time, and lower memory footprint compared to baselines across mesh resolutions.
weaknesses: Scope primarily focused on wave-like and structural mechanics: The formulation naturally aligns with hyperbolic/wave-type and elastodynamic systems where kinetic and potential energies interact across cochains. It remains less clear how seamlessly MeshFT-Net extends to non-conservative advection-dominated problems (such as high-Reynolds-number Navier-Stokes flows with substantial material transport and turbulent mixing).

State-independent interconnection restriction: The primary neural implementation relies on Corollary 3.4 (state-independent incidence coupling), which simplifies the architecture but pushes all nonlinearities into metric and dissipation blocks. Although a state-dependent interconnection ablation is provided in Section 5.7, the main framework primarily addresses quasi-linear or fixed-geometry settings.

Smoothing of high frequencies on complex datasets: In the acoustic scattering benchmark from The Well (Section 5.4), the predicted fields exhibit noticeable smoothing of high-frequency details and reduced peak amplitude contrast compared to the ground truth.

strengths: Principled and elegant theoretical foundation: The local reduction theorem (Theorem 3.3) rigorously deduces a port-Hamiltonian structure at the Jacobian level from four minimal physical axioms (locality, permutation equivariance, orientation covariance, and passivity), rather than postulating a global template ad hoc.

Clear separation of concerns: Grounded in discrete exterior calculus (DEC), the framework cleanly decouples topological incidence structure (fixed and metric-independent) from constitutive and dissipative properties (learned metric/Hodge star operators), effectively eliminating non-physical degrees of freedom.

Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation: The empirical validation spans analytic wave benchmarks, dissipative dynamics, out-of-distribution shifts (frequency, wave speed, resolution transfer), realistic acoustic scattering from The Well, and nonlinear lattice models.

Exceptional physical fidelity and conservation: MeshFT-Net demonstrates orders-of-magnitude improvements in energy conservation, PDE residual minimization, dispersion accuracy, and momentum conservation over unconstrained and penalty-based baselines (MGN, MGN-HP, PI-MGN, HNN, FNO, GraphCON).

Computational efficiency: By exploiting sparse incidence matrices and local metric MLPs, MeshFT-Net achieves linear O(N) complexity, significantly faster training/inference runtimes, and a much smaller memory footprint than standard message-passing GNNs.
weaknesses: Limited evaluation on large-scale 3D or fluid problems: While benchmarks are diverse, experiments are predominantly restricted to 2D domains with relatively modest mesh resolutions (up to ~2.2k nodes). Standard learned mesh simulators (e.g., MeshGraphNets) frequently handle large-scale 3D aerodynamics, cloth drape, or complex deformable solids.

Simplicity of the practical neural instantiation compared to the general theory: While Theorem 3.3 accommodates general nonlinear port-Hamiltonian systems, the primary neural realization (MeshFT-Net) assumes quadratic storage and state-independent conservative coupling J (Corollary 3.4). Applying the framework to large-deformation Lagrangian mechanics or Eulerian advection (where the underlying metric/mesh or convective transport evolves dynamically) remains unaddressed in the primary experiments.

Comparison with prior discrete exterior calculus learning: While the paper positions itself clearly against GNNs and Hamiltonian neural networks, it omits direct empirical comparisons with existing data-driven discrete exterior calculus architectures (e.g., Trask et al., 2022), which also fix incidence matrices and learn discrete Hodge stars.

strengths: Principled and clear theoretical foundation: The paper presents a formal derivation showing that minimal physical assumptions (locality, permutation equivariance, orientation covariance, and incremental energy balance/passivity) necessitate a local port-Hamiltonian Jacobian reduction on cell complexes, cleanly disentangling topology-wired conservative interactions from metric-dependent constitutive laws and dissipation.

Well-designed architecture and numerical integration: MeshFT-Net directly operationalizes the reduction theorem by fixing signed incidence matrices ($D_k$) and learning only symmetric positive-definite metric tensors ($G_\theta$) and positive-semidefinite dissipation ($R_\theta$). Combining this with Strang splitting and CFL-aware sub-stepping guarantees non-increasing energy and exact preservation of discrete topological invariants (such as discrete divergence constraints) to machine precision.

Comprehensive and rigorous empirical evaluation: The authors evaluate the method across diverse settings, including 2D periodic wave dynamics (on regular and Delaunay meshes), dissipative plane waves, out-of-distribution (frequency, parameter, resolution) tests, acoustic scattering from The Well, irregular heterogeneous elasticity, and several nonlinear lattice systems (FPU, damped $\phi^4$, Sine-Gordon).

In-depth physics-consistency diagnostics and ablations: The evaluation thoroughly assesses wave-speed error, canonical consistency, PDE residuals, energy equipartition, and momentum conservation. Furthermore, the ablations (Appendices D.7–D.9) methodically isolate each structural assumption (orientation covariance, topology wiring, metric positivity, state-dependent $J$), validating the necessity of each component.
weaknesses: Narrow domain of applicable physical phenomena: While the theoretical reduction is framed as general continuum physics, the implementation and tests are restricted to wave-like, acoustic, and elastodynamic Hamiltonian/port-Hamiltonian systems with canonical conjugate pairs $(z_k, z_{k+1})$. Crucial continuum physics phenomena, such as fluid dynamics with convective/advective terms ($u \cdot \nabla u$), do not fit into this state-independent signed-incidence skew framework without substantial modifications (e.g., upwinding, metric-dependent flux limiters).

Disparity in structural priors compared to baselines: In many of the synthetic wave and lattice benchmarks, MeshFT-Net essentially hard-codes the exact underlying discrete differential operators ($D_0^\top W D_0$) and only needs to optimize a tiny parameter set (642 parameters, compared to >100k for MGN, MGN-HP, and HNN). While this validates the inductive bias, it heavily biases the comparison in favor of MeshFT-Net on problems that exactly mirror the assumed discrete exterior calculus template.

Assumptions underlying the reduction theorem: The proof of Lemma B.1 and Lemma B.2 relies heavily on interface-locality and linearity of the basis operators. For complex nonlinear continuum systems where constitutive behavior couples across multiple cell degrees or non-adjacent entities, the clean separation into state-independent incidence matrices breaks down, requiring state-dependent gains $C_k(z)$ which are only briefly explored.
